feedback.note: Reason is the only means of grasping reality. Rejecting it does not leave another rational method. It means acting regardless of the facts or in contradiction to them. Calling that rejection caution confuses it with care. What works is a different error, pragmatism, because the consequence of the rejection is the loss of any regard for the facts, not a new test.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about the consequence of rejecting reason?
exercises.quote: Reason is man's only means of grasping reality and of acquiring knowledge—and, therefore, the rejection of reason means that men should act regardless of and/or in contradiction to the facts of reality.

choices.text: Rejecting reason leaves the facts in charge and the action rational.
Rejecting reason means adopting whatever works as the new standard of truth.
Rejecting reason means acting with no regard for the facts, or against them.
Rejecting reason means a person becomes unable to move at all.

feedback.quote: Reason is man's only means of grasping reality and of acquiring knowledge—and, therefore, the rejection of reason means that men should act regardless of and/or in contradiction to the facts of reality.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "The Left: Old and New," Return of the Primitive: The Anti-Industrial Revolution, 162
feedback.note: The therefore is part of the claim. If reason is the only means of grasping reality, rejecting it means acting regardless of the facts, or in contradiction to them, or both. What works is not the consequence the passage draws. Paralysis is not either. The error of calling the rejection harmless caution leaves out the therefore, because no other means of knowledge remains.

exercises.prompt: A council likes a policy, refuses to read the casualty figures, and votes the policy in. Which consequence of rejecting reason is this?

choices.text: Reason applied to the figures, with the vote used only to record the result
A contradiction openly chosen because the figures were judged false on evidence
Mysticism avoided, because no one mentioned a revelation
Action regardless of the facts. The figures were not allowed to count

feedback.note: Refusing the figures is action with no regard for the facts. That is one of the two consequences of rejecting reason. It does not require a positive creed that the figures are the opposite of what they are. The disregard is enough. Calling the scene free of mysticism misses the point, because the failure is the rejection of the only means of knowledge, whatever substitute fills the gap.

exercises.prompt: Match each policy to the relation it has to the facts.

pairs.left: Reading the figures and acting accordingly
pairs.right: Reason, the means of grasping the facts
Action regardless of the facts

pairs.left: Doing the opposite of what the figures show, on a hunch
pairs.right: Action in contradiction to the facts

pairs.left: Calling the refusal a higher standard of truth
pairs.right: A disguise for the rejection, not a new means of knowledge

feedback.note: Reason grasps the facts and acts on that grasp. Refusal to consult them is the "regardless" half. A hunch that reverses them is the "in contradiction" half. Both are what the rejection of reason licenses. Naming the refusal a higher standard does not create a means of knowledge, because no such second means exists.

exercises.prompt: Complete the two forms of action that follow the rejection of reason.

parts.text: Rejecting reason means acting regardless of the facts, or
them.

feedback.note: The rejection licenses action regardless of the facts or against them. "From," "by," and "through" would keep the facts as the guide, which is reason, not its rejection. Against names the contradiction with the facts. Regardless names the refusal to consult them. Either one follows because reason was the only means of grasping reality.

exercises.prompt: Someone says, "I am not contradicting the facts. I am simply not consulting them." Which half of the consequence has he admitted?

choices.text: The regardless half. Ignoring the facts is already the rejection at work
Neither half. Only an open contradiction counts, so indifference is innocent
The knowledge half. Not looking is a new means of knowledge
The pragmatist half. Not looking shows that truth is whatever works

feedback.note: The consequence is stated with and/or: regardless of the facts, or in contradiction to them, or both. Refusing to consult the facts is the regardless clause. It does not become innocent by avoiding an explicit reversal. The error treats only open contradiction as costly, because it leaves out action that simply proceeds with no regard for reality.

exercises.prompt: A leader contradicts the figures on purpose because a feeling says the policy is kind. Which errors are combined?

choices.text: Reason, followed by a check of the feeling against the figures
Mysticism in the means, and action in contradiction to the facts
Skepticism only, with no claim that the feeling knows anything
A valid second means of knowledge, since kindness is a fact the figures missed

feedback.note: The feeling is being used as proof, which is mysticism, a bypass of sensory evidence. The action then contradicts the figures. That is the cost of rejecting reason, not a discovery that kindness revealed a fact the count had hidden. Emotion is not a tool of cognition, because what one feels reports an estimate, not the casualties.

exercises.prompt: Build the consequence that follows when reason is rejected.

feedback.note: Rejecting reason means acting regardless of the facts or against them. Obedience to the facts would be the use of reason, not its rejection. A second reason does not appear to fill the gap, because reason was the only means of grasping reality. The cost is action cut off from the facts, not a gentler method of knowing them.

exercises.prompt: Three answers are on the table: reason, mysticism, and skepticism. What does each say about knowledge?

choices.text: All three say knowledge is impossible, and they differ only in tone, reason included as the confident version
Mysticism says knowledge is impossible, and skepticism offers revelation, the two rivals having swapped their claims
Reason: it is possible by integrating evidence. Mysticism: by bypassing evidence. Skepticism: it is not possible
Reason says truth is whatever works, and the other two deny action, usefulness left standing as the only means

feedback.note: Reason holds that knowledge is possible and that its means is the identification and integration of sensory evidence. Mysticism claims a means that bypasses that evidence. Skepticism denies that knowledge is possible. Swapping the last two confuses a positive non-sensory claim with a denial. Pragmatism is a fourth error, not the name of reason.

exercises.prompt: Sort these three episodes: a sealed revelation, a denial that any measurement can be known, and a measurement checked against the instrument.

choices.text: All three are reason, at different volumes
The denial is mysticism, the revelation is skepticism, and the instrument is a vote
The instrument is mysticism because it was built by people
Revelation is mysticism, the denial is skepticism, and the checked measurement is reason

feedback.note: A revelation sealed against observation claims knowledge by bypassing sensory evidence. That is mysticism. Denying that any measurement can be known is skepticism. Checking the instrument and integrating the result is reason. The swap in the third choice confuses the two rivals, because one offers a non-sensory means and the other denies the possibility of knowledge.

exercises.prompt: A speaker says the mind's forms constitute phenomena, so things as they are cannot be known, and he offers no revelation in their place. Where does the claim belong?

choices.text: With skepticism, as the noumenal result, not as a non-sensory means of knowledge
With mysticism, because unknowability is a kind of faith, denial passed off as faith
With reason, because forms are a method of integrating evidence, objects constituted
With pragmatism, because the forms are said to work, success being all the forms claim

feedback.note: The claim does not offer faith, revelation, or feeling as a route to things as they are. It concludes that those things stay unknowable. That is a skeptical result. Classifying it as mysticism confuses a denial of knowledge with a claimed alternative means. Reason rejects the result, because the senses are contact with reality, not a barrier that manufactures it.

exercises.prompt: Match each sentence to the answer about knowledge it expresses.

pairs.left: Check the evidence and integrate it
pairs.right: Reason: knowledge by the only means

pairs.left: A vision proves the bridge will fail
pairs.right: Mysticism: feeling or revelation used as proof
Skepticism: knowledge is not possible

pairs.left: The reading is true because the project succeeded
pairs.right: Pragmatism: success substituted for the standard of truth

feedback.note: Reason, mysticism, and skepticism give three answers: knowledge by evidence, knowledge by a bypass, and no knowledge. Success as the standard is pragmatism, a further substitute, because what works is not the recognition of reality. The vision does not become reason by being vivid. Vividness is not sensory evidence integrated by a method.

exercises.prompt: Complete the three-way contrast in the order reason, mysticism, skepticism.

parts.text: Reason integrates evidence. Mysticism bypasses it. Skepticism says knowledge is

feedback.note: Skepticism says knowledge is impossible. Easy would describe a success of reason, not a denial. Voted would be subjectivism, and felt would be mysticism, a feeling used as proof. The three answers stay distinct because one affirms a means tied to evidence, one affirms a means that bypasses evidence, and one affirms no knowledge.

exercises.prompt: "I know by revelation that reason cannot know anything." Which description fits the whole sentence?

choices.text: Reason, because a revelation is sensory evidence that has been integrated
Mysticism supplies the means, and skepticism is the content
Skepticism alone, because a revelation is just a way of admitting ignorance
Neither, because a vote could validate both the message and the denial

feedback.note: The means is revelation, a bypass of sensory evidence, so the route is mystical. The content is that reason cannot know, which is a skeptical thesis. Neither label alone covers the sentence. Treating the revelation as an admission of ignorance misses the claim to know, because the speaker is not suspending judgment. He is asserting a conclusion by a non-sensory means.

exercises.prompt: An instrument reading contradicts the other evidence, and someone says the reading is true because the machine is expensive and impressive. Which error is this, if it is not the three main answers?

choices.text: Reason, because expense is a measurement of the facts, price settling the reading
Skepticism, because a contradiction shows knowledge is impossible, knowledge ended
Pragmatism, or a close cousin: a substitute standard in place of identification
Mysticism, because an impressive machine is a revelation, price replacing the evidence

feedback.note: The case is not reason, which would resolve the contradiction by further identification. It is not skepticism, which would deny knowledge rather than crown the expensive reading. It is not mysticism unless a non-sensory faculty is being claimed. The error puts a stand-in, impressiveness or success, in place of the recognition of reality, because the standard of truth remains reason.

exercises.prompt: Build the line that keeps the three answers in one contrast.

feedback.note: Reason knows by evidence, mysticism bypasses the evidence, and skepticism denies knowledge. A vote would be subjectivism, not one of the three. Whatever works would be pragmatism, another substitute standard. The contrast stays clean only if each answer is stated by what it says about whether and how one can know, because mixed labels hide which claim is actually being made.

exercises.prompt: What is logic, stated so that both of its halves are included?

choices.text: A feeling that a sentence is clear, emotion certifying words that name no fact
Whatever works, whether or not it identifies a fact, a useful error counting as logic
A game of consistent words about no fact at all, consistent emptiness being enough
The art of identifying what is, and of keeping those identifications free of contradiction

feedback.note: Logic is the art of non-contradictory identification. Both halves are required: one identifies what is, and one refuses contradiction. A feeling of clarity is not that art, because emotion is not a tool of cognition. What works is pragmatism. Consistent words that identify nothing keep the form and drop the facts.

exercises.prompt: Why call logic an art, rather than an automatic stamp or a gift?

choices.text: Because it is a method one practices by choice, not a stamp the mind applies with no effort
Because the facts rearrange themselves whenever the art is skipped, the tank rewritten
Because only a revelation can perform an identification, the art delivered without any look
Because an art is a contradiction maintained on purpose, the art consisting in holding the clash

feedback.note: An art is a method a person chooses to practice. Logic is that kind of method: non-contradictory identification. It is not an automatic stamp, which would be determinism about thinking, and it is not a revelation, which would be mysticism. Maintaining a contradiction is the abandonment of the art, because the art exists to keep identifications free of clash.

exercises.prompt: A paragraph never contradicts itself and never mentions a single fact. How much of logic does it contain?

choices.text: All of it. Non-contradiction is enough, and identification is optional, empty peace included
None that matters. Without identification there is nothing logic can keep consistent
All of it, if the paragraph feels orderly, a tidy feeling supplying every missing fact
Half, and the missing half can be supplied by a vote, a vote supplying the identification

feedback.note: Logic is non-contradictory identification, so a text that identifies nothing has not practiced it. Verbal peace among empty sentences is a symbol game. A feeling of order does not supply the missing facts, because emotion is not cognition. A vote does not either. The error keeps one word of the art and drops the act of identifying what is.

exercises.prompt: Match each performance to the part of logic it honors or drops.

pairs.left: Naming the fact and refusing the clash
pairs.right: Both halves of the art: identification and non-contradiction

pairs.left: A clear feeling and no fact
pairs.right: Identification dropped. Emotion is not a substitute

pairs.left: A tidy story about no warehouse
pairs.right: Non-contradiction kept, identification dropped
Non-contradiction dropped, so the art is abandoned

feedback.note: The art requires both identification of what is and freedom from contradiction. A feeling drops the identification and offers mysticism in its place, because a feeling is not evidence. A tidy empty story keeps only the verbal half. Retaining a clash drops non-contradiction, which is the other half of the same art.

exercises.prompt: Complete the name of the art that objectivity uses.

parts.text: Logic is the art of non-contradictory

feedback.quote: Logic is the art of non-contradictory identification.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, Galt's Speech, For the New Intellectual, 125
feedback.note: Logic is the art of non-contradictory identification. Invention would write the facts instead of identifying them, which is subjectivism. Feeling is not a means of knowledge. Success is pragmatism, a substitute standard, because what works does not decide what is. The art identifies reality and does not contradict the identification.

exercises.prompt: Which omission destroys the art even if the other half is loudly praised?

choices.text: Neither. Praising one half is the whole art, so praise of consistency excuses a text that identifies nothing
Only the omission of a feeling, which is the real third half, logic failing unless that feeling is added
Either omission. Identification without non-contradiction, or non-contradiction without identification, is not logic
Only the omission of a vote, which makes identifications official, the art waiting on a group's ratification

feedback.note: The two halves are one art. Identifying while keeping a contradiction is not logic, and avoiding contradiction while identifying nothing is not logic either. The error treats the phrase as a menu. A feeling or a vote is not a third half, because neither identifies what is. Both are substitutes for the art rather than parts of it.

exercises.prompt: A navigator identifies the reef from the chart and the lookout, then adds a second claim that the channel is clear of that reef. What must he do to remain logical?

choices.text: Keep both claims, because a contradiction shows thoroughness, contradiction preserved
Drop the chart, because identification is optional once words agree, words saved
Let the more hopeful claim stand, because usefulness is logic, hope declared real
Give up one claim. He cannot identify the reef and deny it in the same respect

feedback.note: He has identified a reef and then contradicted the identification. Logic will not let both stand. Keeping them praises a clash. Dropping the chart drops the identification in order to save the words. Usefulness is pragmatism. The art requires him to resolve the contradiction, because non-contradictory identification cannot affirm the reef and the empty channel together.

exercises.prompt: Build the demand that keeps both halves of logic in one act.

feedback.note: Logic identifies what is and refuses the contradiction. Following a feeling would drop the identification, because emotion is not a tool of cognition. Either half alone is not the art. A tidy clash, or a clear feeling, fails for the same reason: one of the two requirements has been left out.

exercises.prompt: What does logic do when it identifies a fact that is already there?

choices.text: It names facts that are already there. It does not invent them or swap them for a wish
It writes the facts so that a wish will come out true, the wish rewritten into the fact
It names a feeling and calls the feeling the fact, the feeling put in the tank's place
It withholds every name, because naming would change the fact, silence preferred to identity

feedback.note: Consciousness is identification, and existence is identity. Logic names what is. It does not decree it. Writing the facts to save a wish is subjectivism. Naming a feeling as if it were the fact is mysticism, because emotion is not a tool of cognition. Refusing to name anything is not a purer logic. It is the refusal to identify.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about existence and about consciousness?
exercises.quote: Existence is Identity, Consciousness is Identification.

choices.text: Existence waits to receive an identity from the mind that names it.
To exist is to be something, and consciousness identifies what exists.
Consciousness is a feeling, and identity is whatever the feeling prefers.
Identification is optional, because a thing can exist as nothing in particular.

feedback.quote: Existence is Identity, Consciousness is Identification.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, Galt's Speech, For the New Intellectual, 124
feedback.note: The passage states two corollaries together. Existence is identity: to be is to be something. Consciousness is identification of that something, not the author of it. A mind that assigns identity is subjectivism. A feeling that prefers an identity is mysticism. A thing that is nothing in particular is not a thing, because to exist is to be something.

exercises.prompt: A pilot wants the fog to be clear and reports "clear" without looking. What has he swapped for an identification?

choices.text: A look at the field, which would have named what is there
A contradiction he discovered in the field itself
A wish. The report names what he wants, not what the field is
A measurement that conflicted with the wish and was kept

feedback.note: Identification names the field as it is. The report names the field as he wishes it to be. That swap is subjectivism, because the mind is writing the fact instead of identifying it. Looking would have been the start of an identification. A wish does not become one by being spoken in the vocabulary of a report.

exercises.prompt: Match each act to what it does with a fact.

pairs.left: Reporting the gauge as it reads
pairs.right: Identification: naming a fact that is there

pairs.left: Reporting the gauge as one needs it to read
pairs.right: A wish substituted for an identification

pairs.left: Reporting one's fear as the reading
pairs.right: Mysticism: a feeling offered as the fact

pairs.left: Changing the gauge by an actual repair
pairs.right: A real change in the object, which a later identification can then name

feedback.note: Logic identifies what is. It does not swap a wish or a fear for the reading, because neither is the gauge. A repair is different: it changes the object by a real action, and the new reading is then a new fact to identify. Subjectivism pretends the report itself was the repair. It was not.

exercises.prompt: Complete the corollary that says what consciousness does.

parts.text: Consciousness is

feedback.quote: Existence is Identity, Consciousness is Identification.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, Galt's Speech, For the New Intellectual, 124
feedback.note: Consciousness is identification. Invention would make it the author of identity, which contradicts the corollary that existence is identity. Neutrality would refuse to identify. Feeling is not the act, because an emotion reports an estimate of the facts rather than the facts. Logic is the art of performing the identification without contradiction.

exercises.prompt: A contract exists because the parties chose to make it. Does identifying the contract create it a second time?

choices.text: Yes. Every identification rewrites the fact it names, so the naming brings a second contract into force
Yes. A man-made fact has no identity until a feeling approves it, approval required before the contract exists
No. Man-made facts cannot be identified at all, so contracts, marriages, and laws stay outside cognition
No. The choice made a fact. The identification names that fact. It does not wish a second contract into being

feedback.note: The parties' choice brought a man-made fact into existence. Identification then names it. The naming does not create an extra contract, and it does not mean man-made facts are unknowable. The error treats every identification as a decree, because it will not distinguish making a fact by action from knowing a fact by logic.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is an identification, and which is a wish wearing the same grammar?

choices.text: "The tank is empty" after a look is an identification. "The tank is empty" said to make it so is a wish
Both are identifications, because both use the verb "is", the wish counting as the same act as the look
Both are wishes, because every report is a preference, so a gauge reading is only a preference about the level
Neither can be told apart, because facts have no identity, a look and a wish being equally mute

feedback.note: Grammar does not decide. The first sentence names a fact the look delivered. The second tries to use the same words as a decree. Logic is the first act, not the second. Calling every report a preference is subjectivism, because it denies that consciousness identifies an identity that is already there. The wish does not empty the tank.

exercises.prompt: Build the corollary that keeps consciousness from writing reality.

feedback.quote: Existence is Identity, Consciousness is Identification.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, Galt's Speech, For the New Intellectual, 124
feedback.note: Existence is identity, and consciousness is identification. A wish or an invention would make consciousness the author of identity, which is subjectivism. Logic names what is. It does not swap a preferred identity for the one the facts have, because to exist is already to be something specific.

exercises.prompt: What does the principle of non-contradiction forbid a thing to be?

choices.text: Any thing having more than one attribute, even in different respects, complexity forbidden
The same thing being two incompatible things at the same time and in the same respect
Any change across time, as if a later state contradicted an earlier one, history contradicted
A difference in measurement between two units of one concept, different heights forbidden

feedback.note: The same thing cannot be two incompatible things at the same time and in the same respect. A thing may have many attributes in different respects, and it may change over time. Those are not contradictions. Different measurements are how similar units fall under one concept. The error treats complexity, or change, as if it were a clash of identity.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about a leaf and incompatible states?
exercises.quote: A leaf cannot be a stone at the same time, it cannot be all red and all green at the same time, it cannot freeze and burn at the same time.

choices.text: A leaf may be all red and all green at the same time if the description is useful.
A leaf cannot be red in one season and green in another.
A leaf cannot be incompatible things at the same time.
A leaf cannot be partly red and partly green.

feedback.quote: A leaf cannot be a stone at the same time, it cannot be all red and all green at the same time, it cannot freeze and burn at the same time.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, Galt's Speech, For the New Intellectual, 125
feedback.note: The passage forbids incompatible identities at the same time: stone and leaf, all red and all green, freezing and burning. It does not forbid change across seasons, and it does not forbid a leaf that is partly one color and partly another. Those are different times or different respects. Usefulness would not license the clash, because pragmatism is not non-contradiction.

exercises.prompt: A leaf is red at the edge and green at the center, now. Is that a contradiction?

choices.text: Yes. Any two colors on one leaf violate identity, parts counting as one respect
Yes. "Same respect" is a verbal trick, and parts do not count, complexity barred
Yes, unless a vote assigns the leaf a single official color, color by ballot
No. The colors are in different respects. It is not all red and all green

feedback.note: All red and all green at the same time would be incompatible. Red at the edge and green at the center are different respects, or different parts, of one leaf. The error drops "the same respect" and then forbids every complexity, because a thing with two attributes is not a thing with two incompatible identities. A vote does not decide the colors.

exercises.prompt: Match each description to the verdict non-contradiction gives it.

pairs.left: All red and all green now
pairs.right: A contradiction: incompatible in the same respect at the same time

pairs.left: Red at the edge, green at the center
pairs.right: Not a contradiction: different respects
Not a contradiction: different times

pairs.left: A stone and a leaf at once
pairs.right: A contradiction: two incompatible identities

feedback.note: Non-contradiction forbids incompatible identities at the same time and in the same respect. All red and all green is that clash, and so is stone and leaf. A difference of part, or a difference of time, is a real difference, not a broken identity. The error treats every complexity as a contradiction, because it drops the qualifiers the principle includes.

exercises.prompt: Complete the two qualifiers in the principle of non-contradiction.

parts.text: Not two incompatible things at the same time and in the same

feedback.note: The qualifiers are the same time and the same respect. A wish, a vote, or a mood is not a respect in which a fact contradicts itself. Those are attempts to soften a clash by subjectivism or by mysticism, because an incompatible pair at one time in one respect is an error in thinking, not a fact the leaf can have.

exercises.prompt: A door is open at noon and shut at night. Someone calls the day a contradiction. What qualifier did he drop?

choices.text: Time. The door is not open and shut at the same time
Identity. A door may be a window if the schedule is tight
Evidence. The hinge was never perceived
Nothing. Change across a day is the same as being both states at once

feedback.note: Open at noon and shut at night are two states at two times. That is change, not a contradiction. The error drops "at the same time" and then treats a history as a clash. A door does not become a window by schedule. The principle forbids incompatible states together, because identity is what a thing is, not a ban on its acting through time.

exercises.prompt: Which repair correctly saves a seeming clash without pretending the clash is real?

choices.text: Say the leaf is all red and all green, and call the clash a higher truth
Specify the part or the time, and show that the incompatibles were not together
Say the colors are whatever works for the painter
Deny that the leaf has any color, so no respect remains

feedback.note: A seeming clash is repaired by finding a difference of time or of respect, when there is one. If the leaf really is all red and all green now, the identifications cannot both stand. Calling the clash a higher truth abandons non-contradiction. What works is pragmatism. Denying the color evades the percept, because the repair has to identify the leaf, not erase it.

exercises.prompt: Build the principle with both qualifiers in place.

feedback.note: A thing cannot be both of two incompatibles at the same time and in the same respect. Extending the ban to any time in history would forbid change. Extending it to every respect at once would forbid a complex thing. Both extensions drop a qualifier, because the principle is about one identity clashing with itself, not about difference as such.

exercises.prompt: When two of your conclusions contradict, where is the contradiction?

choices.text: In the facts, which sometimes have incompatible identities
Nowhere. A contradiction is a higher truth one should keep
In the thinking. Reality does not contradict itself
In the senses, which invented one of the facts at will

feedback.note: To arrive at a contradiction is to confess an error in one's thinking. The facts are what they are, and a thing cannot be two incompatibles at the same time and in the same respect. Calling the clash a feature of reality misplaces the error. Calling it a higher truth abandons identification. The senses did not invent either fact, because the organs have no volition to distort.

exercises.prompt: Two instruments report one tank as entirely full and entirely empty at the same moment. What should you conclude about the tank?

choices.text: The tank has no identity until the reports are averaged, cured by a number neither gauge gave
The tank is both, and the contradiction is a discovery about liquids, liquids allowed to be both at once
The tank is whatever the more anxious reading feels like, anxiety replacing both gauges
The tank is something. At least one identification, or the claim that they are simultaneous, has failed

feedback.note: The tank cannot be entirely full and entirely empty at once in the same respect. The contradiction confesses an error in the thinking, because a bad reading, a misunderstood word, or two times treated as one is a fault in the identification. It is not a discovery that liquids contradict themselves.

exercises.prompt: A tradition says a contradiction in one's conclusions shows that reality itself contains the contradiction. What is being denied?

choices.text: That a contradiction is an error in thinking rather than a feature of the facts
Nothing. Reality is the sort of thing that can be A and non-A together, as a fact
The possibility that a reading can be mistaken, no reading allowed to be wrong
That two times can differ without clashing, change across an hour forbidden

feedback.note: Identity means a thing is what it is. A contradiction in the conclusions is a confession that the thinking went wrong, not a report that the thing has incompatible identities. The tradition denies that placement of the error. It treats a failure of identification as a metaphysical discovery, because it will not let the law of identity judge the conclusions.

exercises.prompt: Match each response to the place it puts the contradiction.

pairs.right: In the thinking, where an error can be found

pairs.left: Announce that the tank is both full and empty
pairs.right: In reality, as if identity had failed

pairs.left: Call the clash a profound truth
pairs.right: Nowhere one must correct. The mind is told to keep it

pairs.left: Blame the eye for inventing a reading
pairs.right: In the senses, which have no volition to invent

feedback.note: The contradiction is an error in thinking, so the readings are what one rechecks. Putting it in the tank denies identity. Calling it profound keeps the error as if it were knowledge. Blaming the eye confuses a misidentification with a lying sense, because the organs do not invent their objects. The confession belongs to the mind that produced the clash.

exercises.prompt: Complete the placement of a contradiction.

parts.text: A contradiction is an error in one's

feedback.note: A contradiction is an error in one's thinking, not in the facts, not in the senses, and not in one's feelings. The facts do not contradict themselves. The senses have no volition to invent a clash. A feeling may accompany the discovery and still is not the error, because the error is the pair of identifications that cannot both be true.

exercises.prompt: The two reports turn out to be an hour apart. The tank was filled in between. Was there a contradiction in reality?

choices.text: Yes. Change over an hour is a contradiction the world committed, a later filling having broken the tank
No. What looked like a contradiction was a difference in time, and the thinking had dropped that qualifier
Yes. Once two sentences clash on paper, reality has clashed, whatever the clock says, the clock irrelevant
No. The hour proves that contradictions are a higher form of truth, and the mind should preserve the clash

feedback.note: Full at one time and empty at another is change, not a broken identity. The apparent contradiction came from dropping "at the same time" in the thinking. Finding that out is how the confession of error does its work. It is not a discovery that the tank violated its nature, and it is not a reason to cherish clashes, because the clash dissolved when the times were specified.

exercises.prompt: At the first sign of a clash, someone discards every claim he has ever made. What has he done with the confession?

choices.text: He has located the error and corrected that identification
He has shown that reality contradicts itself only on Tuesdays
He has turned one error into skepticism about knowledge as such
He has kept both sides, which is the proper use of a contradiction

feedback.note: Arriving at a contradiction confesses an error in thinking. The proper use is to find which identification failed. Discarding every claim treats one clash as proof that knowledge is impossible, which is skepticism. The error overshoots the confession, because a local failure of identification is not a failure of the fact that things are what they are.

exercises.prompt: Build the placement that keeps the contradiction out of the facts.

feedback.note: A contradiction is an error in thinking, not in reality. Calling it a feature of the facts moves the failure out of the mind and into identity, which identity cannot contain. The same thing cannot be incompatibles at the same time and in the same respect. The confession tells you to correct the thinking, because the facts did not break.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between finding a contradiction and maintaining one?

choices.text: Finding it is the failure. Maintaining it is the cure, maintenance praised as knowledge
They are the same act, and both should be prolonged, exposure and surrender as one act
Finding it rewrites the facts. Maintaining it restores them, clash as restoration
Finding it exposes an error. Maintaining it gives up the mind's hold on the facts

feedback.note: To arrive at a contradiction is to confess an error in one's thinking. That confession is how logic exposes the error. To maintain the contradiction is to abdicate the mind and leave reality. The error of treating maintenance as a cure keeps the clash as if it were knowledge, because a mind that affirms incompatibles has given up identification.

exercises.prompt: What do the two halves of this passage establish, taken together?
exercises.quote: To arrive at a contradiction is to confess an error in one's thinking; to maintain a contradiction is to abdicate one's mind and to evict oneself from the realm of reality.

choices.text: Finding a contradiction exposes an error. Keeping it abandons the mind's hold on reality.
Both arriving at a contradiction and keeping it are ways of knowing the facts. Both succeed.
A contradiction should be maintained, because the confession is optional. Replace the confession.
Reality includes the contradiction, so the mind is at fault for noticing it. Notice is the fault.

feedback.quote: To arrive at a contradiction is to confess an error in one's thinking; to maintain a contradiction is to abdicate one's mind and to evict oneself from the realm of reality.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, Galt's Speech, For the New Intellectual, 125
feedback.note: The first half places the contradiction in one's thinking: arriving at it is a confession of error. The second half names the further failure of maintaining it, which abdicates the mind. Treating both halves as knowledge drops the confession. Blaming reality for the clash denies identity, because the error was in the thinking, and keeping it is how one leaves the facts behind.

exercises.prompt: A scientist finds two results that clash, rechecks, and withdraws the faulty reading. A colleague publishes both as final and says each is true in its own narrative. Who has done what?

choices.text: The scientist maintained the clash. The colleague found the error
The scientist used the contradiction to expose an error. The colleague maintained it
Both maintained it, because any rechecking is a kind of loyalty to contradiction
The colleague adhered to the facts by giving each result a story

feedback.note: Rechecking and withdrawing the faulty reading is what the confession is for. Publishing both as final, under two narratives, maintains the contradiction. The stories are subjectivism, because they let incompatible identifications stand by splitting "true" into a private word. The scientist kept the mind's hold on one set of facts. The colleague gave it up.

exercises.prompt: Match each response to the act it performs with a contradiction.

pairs.left: Find the faulty reading and withdraw it
pairs.right: Using a contradiction to expose an error
Maintaining the contradiction

pairs.left: Call both true in different narratives
pairs.right: Subjectivism: the clash is kept by splitting the standard

pairs.left: Discard logic because a clash appeared
pairs.right: Skepticism: one error is treated as the ruin of knowledge

feedback.note: Finding the contradiction should lead to finding the error. Keeping both results maintains the clash and abdicates the identification. Two narratives do the same under subjectivism, because truth is then whatever each story prefers. Discarding logic altogether is skepticism. None of those three is the confession put to work.

exercises.prompt: Complete the consequence of keeping a contradiction.

parts.text: To maintain a contradiction is to abdicate one's

feedback.quote: To arrive at a contradiction is to confess an error in one's thinking; to maintain a contradiction is to abdicate one's mind and to evict oneself from the realm of reality.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, Galt's Speech, For the New Intellectual, 125
feedback.note: Maintaining a contradiction abdicates the mind. It is not a way of preserving the error as a trophy, nor a way of honoring evidence, nor a form of honest doubt. Doubt, when it has grounds, is a step toward correcting an identification. Maintenance refuses the correction, because one has chosen to affirm what cannot be identified together.

exercises.prompt: Why is "both readings are true for different people" not a resolution?

choices.text: It finds which reading failed and withdraws that one
It specifies a difference of time that dissolves the clash
It maintains the contradiction by making truth depend on who is speaking
It shows the tank changed, so the two readings were never incompatible

feedback.note: A real difference of time or of respect can dissolve a seeming clash, and a faulty reading can be withdrawn. "True for different people" does neither. It keeps both identifications and relocates truth into the speakers. That is subjectivism, and it maintains the contradiction, because the tank is still being called incompatible things with no difference in the tank.

exercises.prompt: Which response finds the contradiction and does not maintain it, and also does not throw out the method?

choices.text: Keep both readings and praise the clash, both readings kept as knowledge
Declare that logic fails whenever readings differ, logic retired with the bad reading
Average the readings and call the average what works, an average put in place of the report
Locate the failed identification, correct it, and keep non-contradiction as the method

feedback.note: The proper response uses the contradiction as a confession and then removes the error. Praising the clash maintains it. Declaring that logic fails is skepticism, which evicts the method along with the bad reading. Averaging is pragmatism, a substitute standard, because the task is to identify the tank, not to manufacture a third number that saves both sentences.

exercises.prompt: Build the contrast between the two things one can do with a contradiction.

feedback.note: Finding a contradiction exposes an error in thinking. Maintaining it abandons the facts, which is the abdication of the mind. Calling the clash a higher truth is the maintenance under another name, because one has stopped identifying and started keeping incompatibles. The confession is useful only if it leads to correcting the error rather than preserving it.

exercises.prompt: What is a context of knowledge, as distinct from a mood or a story?

choices.text: The body of facts and earlier ideas a claim depends on, not a mood or a private story
A mood that makes the claim feel settled, that feeling serving as the facts depended on
A private story in which the claim is true for the speaker, the story replacing those facts
A vote that adopts the claim for this occasion, agreement serving as the whole context

feedback.note: A context of knowledge is the body of facts and earlier ideas a claim depends on. A mood is not that body, because a feeling reports an estimate rather than the facts. A private story is subjectivism, truth relocated into a narrative. A vote does not supply the dependence either. The context is what gives the claim its meaning.

exercises.prompt: Someone says a dose is toxic. Which items are the context that claim depends on?

choices.text: The speaker's anxiety, and nothing about the substance, alarm replacing the substance and the dose
The substance, the amount, and the kind of organism, together with what is known about them
A story in which the same dose is harmless because the speaker prefers it, preference overriding it
The word toxic, used with no facts attached, the sound replacing substance, amount, and organism

feedback.note: The claim depends on facts: which substance, how much, and for what kind of living thing, plus the earlier knowledge of what those facts do. Anxiety is not that context, because emotion is not evidence. A preferred story that cancels the dose is subjectivism. The bare word, cut off from those facts, has no context and no meaning one can use.

exercises.prompt: The same substance at a much smaller dose is harmless. What changed?

choices.text: Nothing. Context is a mood, and the mood was constant, amount irrelevant
The word, which now means its opposite by stipulation, dose left unchanged
A fact the claim depends on. A different amount is a different context
Reality, which contradicts itself whenever doses differ, identity broken

feedback.note: Amount is one of the facts the toxicity claim depends on. Change the amount and the context of the claim has changed. That is not a mood and not a stipulation about the word. It is also not a contradiction in reality, because different amounts are different facts, not one fact with two incompatible identities. Context tracks those facts.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to the role it plays, or fails to play, as context.

pairs.left: The substance, the dose, and the organism
pairs.right: The facts a toxicity claim depends on

pairs.left: Earlier knowledge of what the substance does
pairs.right: The prior ideas the claim also depends on
Not a context. An estimate, not the facts

pairs.left: A story in which the dose is harmless at will
pairs.right: Subjectivism: a private narrative in place of the facts

feedback.note: Context is the body of facts and earlier ideas the claim depends on. The substance, the dose, the organism, and what is already known about them are that body. Alarm is an emotion, not a context, because a feeling does not establish toxicity. A story that cancels the dose at will is subjectivism. It keeps the word and drops the facts.

exercises.prompt: Complete the description of a context of knowledge.

parts.text: A context is the body of facts and earlier ideas a claim
on.

feedback.note: A claim depends on a body of facts and earlier ideas, and that body is its context. Votes, feelings, and wishes do not make a context, because they do not supply the facts that give the claim meaning. Treating them as the context is subjectivism or mysticism, a replacement of knowledge by preference or by feeling.

exercises.prompt: Someone says, "In my context the dose is not toxic," and names no different fact. What has he used the word to do?

choices.text: To record a smaller dose, which would be a real change of context, toxicity actually changing
To restate a definition while keeping the same units, the referents held fixed
To trace a later conclusion back to the evidence it rests on, substance and organism named
To shelter a wish. No new fact has changed the body of knowledge the claim depends on

feedback.note: A real change of context is a change in the facts or in the knowledge the claim depends on, such as a different dose. "My context," with no such change, is a private story. The error is subjectivism, because context has been turned into a framing that protects a preference. The toxicity still depends on the substance, the amount, and the organism.

exercises.prompt: Which distinction keeps context from becoming a license to say anything?

choices.text: A different context means different relevant facts, not a different reality invented to save the sentence
Context means the speaker's sincerity, so a sincere claim has a context, sincerity making the dose harmless
Context means the latest mood, so the claim changes when the mood does, the mood resetting toxicity
Context means a vote, so the group's framing is the body of facts, the vote making the dose safe

feedback.note: Contexts differ when the facts or the earlier knowledge differ. They do not differ by sincerity, mood, or vote. Those substitutes invent a second reality for the sentence instead of naming the facts it depends on. The error is subjectivism, because one set of facts cannot be made toxic and harmless by a change of story alone.

exercises.prompt: Build the account of context that keeps it tied to knowledge.

feedback.note: Context is the facts and earlier ideas a claim depends on. A private mood or a convenient story is not that body, because neither is knowledge. Substituting one of them is subjectivism. It keeps the word context and drops the only thing that gives a claim meaning: the facts and the earlier ideas it rests on.

exercises.prompt: What does an order of knowledge forbid you to do with a later item?

choices.text: Let it rest on earlier knowledge, including percepts, the later item drawn from that base
Use it as if it came first, or as if it could cancel the earlier knowledge it rests on
Trace a science back to the concepts and the evidence it required, then checked downward
Correct a later conclusion when it clashes with an earlier fact, the earlier fact retained

feedback.note: Hierarchy is an order: later knowledge rests on earlier knowledge and cannot be used as if it came first. Tracing a science back to its evidence respects that order. So does correcting a later conclusion against an earlier fact. The forbidden move inverts the order, because a dependent item has no content except what the earlier knowledge supplies.

exercises.prompt: What order of dependence does this passage establish?
exercises.quote: Without sensory evidence, there can be no concepts; without concepts, there can be no language; without language, there can be no knowledge and no science.

choices.text: Science comes first and may cancel sensory evidence. The senses lose standing.
Language creates the facts, and the senses illustrate the words. Words make facts.
Sensory evidence, then concepts, then language, then knowledge and science.
Feeling comes before evidence, and science rests on the feeling. Emotion is first.

feedback.quote: Without sensory evidence, there can be no concepts; without concepts, there can be no language; without language, there can be no knowledge and no science.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "Kant Versus Sullivan," Philosophy: Who Needs It, 90
feedback.note: The passage states an order of dependence. Sensory evidence comes before concepts, concepts before language, and language before knowledge and science. Using science as if it came first, or using language as if it created the facts, inverts that order. Feeling is not a step in it, because emotion is not a source of information.

exercises.prompt: A theory is offered as prior to percepts and is then used to argue that percepts are not evidence. What has the order been made to do?

choices.text: Its proper work. Later knowledge is the base of earlier knowledge, earlier facts demoted
A check, in which the theory is traced back to the percepts it needs, denial misnamed
A definitional restatement that keeps the same units, mislabeled as restatement
An inversion. A later item is used as if it came first and could cancel its base

feedback.note: The theory rests on concepts, which rest on sensory evidence. Offering it as prior to percepts, and using it to cancel them, treats the later item as the base. That inverts the order. A real check would trace the theory downward. The error is using dependent knowledge as if it came first, because without the percepts the theory has nothing to be about.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to the place the order gives it.

pairs.right: First. Without it there are no concepts
After evidence, and before language
After concepts, and before knowledge and science
A later item pretending to come first

feedback.note: The order runs from sensory evidence to concepts, to language, to knowledge and science. Each later item rests on the earlier and cannot be used as if it came first. Science deployed against percepts pretends to be the base it actually depends on. That inversion is empty, because the denial uses the very evidence the order says science requires.

exercises.prompt: Complete the first dependence in the order.

parts.text: Without sensory evidence, there can be no

feedback.quote: Without sensory evidence, there can be no concepts; without concepts, there can be no language; without language, there can be no knowledge and no science.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "Kant Versus Sullivan," Philosophy: Who Needs It, 90
feedback.note: Without sensory evidence there are no concepts. Feelings, votes, and revelations are not the next item in the order, because they are not products of identifying sensory material. Putting them first would be mysticism or subjectivism. The order starts with the only source of information and builds later knowledge on it.

exercises.prompt: Why can language not be the base that creates the facts?

choices.text: Language rests on concepts, and concepts rest on sensory evidence. The facts are not a product of the words
Language is first in the order, and evidence is a decoration of grammar, the sentence creating what it names
Words have no dependence, so each word may create the fact it names, senses kept on as illustrations
The order runs backward whenever a sentence is published, publication reversing which one is the base

feedback.note: Language is a later item. It depends on concepts, which depend on sensory evidence of facts that are already there. Treating words as the base inverts the order and slides into subjectivism, because the sentence is then asked to create what it can only name. Publishing does not reverse the dependence.

exercises.prompt: A student learns a scientific formula by heart and cannot say which percepts or earlier concepts it depends on. What has he lost?

choices.text: Nothing. A formula is valid precisely by having no earlier base
The order. He is using a later item as if it came first
The right to check the formula against new evidence
Only the spelling. The order is optional once the symbols are memorized

feedback.note: The formula is later knowledge. If he cannot connect it to earlier concepts and to sensory evidence, he is treating it as a starting point. That violates the hierarchy, because later knowledge rests on earlier knowledge and may not be used as if it came first. Memory of the symbols is not a substitute for that order.

exercises.prompt: Build the rule of order in its shortest form.

feedback.note: Later knowledge rests on earlier knowledge and cannot come first. Letting it cancel or replace the earlier items inverts the order. Science, language, and concepts are later relative to sensory evidence. Using any of them as the base they actually depend on is empty, because the dependence runs in one direction.

exercises.prompt: What is a floating concept, as distinct from a merely wide one?

choices.text: Any concept wider than a single percept, even when it reduces to chairs and tables
A first-level concept formed directly from percepts, abstraction itself counting as detachment
A concept used with no context, cut off from the facts and the order that give it meaning
A definition restated when knowledge deepens, with the units kept, depth cutting the word off

feedback.note: A floating concept is used with no context. It has been cut off from the facts it refers to and from the earlier knowledge it rests on. Width is not the same charge. A wide concept that still reduces to earlier concepts is not floating. A restatement that keeps the units keeps the context. The error is detachment, because meaning depends on that connection.

exercises.prompt: A speaker demands "objectivity" and explains that he means never taking a side, with no facts named. What is the status of the word in his mouth?

choices.text: A concept tied to adherence to stated evidence, indecision still counting as adherence to facts
A first-level percept of objectivity, seen beside the furniture, an entity among the chairs
A contextual certainty about a named body of evidence, the missing facts somehow already settled
A floating concept: the word is cut off from the facts that give objectivity its meaning

feedback.note: Objectivity means volitional adherence to reality by logic. Used to mean chronic indecision, with no facts in view, the word has been cut off from that meaning. It is floating. It is not a percept, and it is not a certainty, because no evidence has been named. The error keeps a prestigious word and drops the context.

exercises.prompt: Which use of "proof" is floating, and which is not?

choices.text: A shout of "proved," with no premises, is floating. A proof that names its evidence is not
Both are floating, because proof is wider than a percept, width alone detaching every proof
The use that names the evidence is floating, and the bare shout is not, naming called floating
Neither can float, because every abstract word is tied to facts automatically, words already tied

feedback.note: "Proved," with no premises and no evidence, is a concept used with no context. A proof that names the evidence and the earlier conclusions it rests on is tied back down. Width does not decide the issue. The error treats every abstraction as floating, or none as floating, because it ignores whether the user can connect the word to facts and to earlier knowledge.

exercises.prompt: Match each use to whether the concept is floating.

pairs.left: "Justice," with no act, no person, and no facts
pairs.right: Floating: cut off from the facts that would give it meaning
Not floating: tied to percepts

pairs.left: "Furniture," connected to table, chair, and bed
pairs.right: Not floating: a wider concept still inside the order

pairs.left: "Certainty," meaning a warm feeling and no evidence
pairs.right: Floating: the word is cut off from the context that defines it

feedback.note: A concept floats when it is used with no context, cut off from facts and from the order of knowledge. "Justice" with no facts, and "certainty" as a mere feeling, are floating. "Table" tied to percepts is not. "Furniture" tied to earlier concepts is not, because abstract is not the same as detached. The connection is what decides.

feedback.note: A floating concept is used with no context, cut off from the facts and the order that give it meaning. Volume, sincerity, and repetition do not supply that context. They leave the word detached. The error treats emphasis as meaning, because a concept means the units it integrates and the earlier knowledge it rests on, not the force with which it is said.

exercises.prompt: Someone says every wide concept floats, because one cannot point to "furniture" as a percept separate from tables and chairs. What has he confused?

choices.text: A floating word with a word that names its evidence, table and furniture charged alike
Hierarchy with detachment. A wider concept is not floating if it rests on earlier concepts
A percept with a contradiction, width treated as a broken identity among the chairs
Nothing. Every concept above a percept is empty by definition, width alone making furniture empty

feedback.note: Furniture is wider than a percept, and it is not floating when one can reduce it to table, chair, and bed, and those to percepts. The charge confuses the hierarchy of concepts with the fault of using a concept and no context. The error leaves out the order, because detachment is the loss of that connection, not the mere fact of width.

exercises.prompt: Which repair is still floating, rather than a return to context?

choices.text: Naming the evidence a proof actually uses, plus the conclusions those premises use
Reducing furniture to the earlier concepts it integrates, down to the percepts
Adding a thicker abstraction, such as "transcendental proof," with no facts added
Stating the facts one calls just or unjust, together with the standard used to judge them

feedback.note: Putting a concept back means reconnecting it to facts and to earlier knowledge. A thicker abstraction, with no facts, moves further away. It is still floating, one level higher. The error treats another detached word as a context, because context is not more emptiness. It is the body of knowledge the word was cut off from.

exercises.prompt: Build the charge that names detachment rather than mere width.

feedback.note: The fault is being used with no context, cut off from the facts. "Wider than a percept, and therefore empty" confuses hierarchy with floating, because a wide concept can remain tied to earlier concepts and through them to percepts. Detachment is the loss of that tie, not the existence of an abstraction.

exercises.prompt: How is a floating concept restored to the knowledge it was cut off from?

choices.text: By saying it more loudly, volume standing in for the missing facts
By adding a thicker word and no facts, the new word doing duty as the facts
By stipulating a new meaning that drops the original units, referents replaced
By naming the facts it refers to and the earlier knowledge it rests on

feedback.note: Restoration names the referents and the earlier knowledge. Emphasis does not do it, because volume is not a context. A thicker word with no facts floats further. A stipulation that drops the units replaces the concept instead of restoring it. The connection to facts and to the order is the whole repair.

exercises.prompt: A speaker says "this is certain" more and more insistently, and names no evidence. What would put the concept back?

choices.text: Naming the evidence and the earlier conclusions the certainty depends on
A still louder repetition
Calling it transcendentally certain, with no facts added
Redefining certainty as a private feeling, and dropping the evidence it used to require

feedback.note: Certainty is contextual: within the evidence, nothing warrants doubt. Putting it back means naming that evidence and the earlier knowledge it rests on. Volume does not name them. A thicker honorific does not either. Redefining the word as a feeling drops the units of the concept, which is a stipulation, not a restoration, because the original meaning has been discarded.

exercises.prompt: Someone uses "proof" with no premises. Which response restores it, rather than decorating it?

choices.text: Repeat "absolutely proved" until the audience is tired
State the evidence and the earlier conclusions the proof uses
Add "in a higher sense," and still name no premise
Stipulate that proof will mean agreement, and drop the evidence

feedback.note: A proof is restored by naming what it depends on: the evidence and the earlier conclusions. Repetition and a higher sense leave it floating. Agreement as a new meaning is subjectivism, and it drops the original units of the concept. The error in the decorations is that they add emphasis or abstraction instead of the facts, because only the facts give the word a context.

exercises.prompt: Match each maneuver to what it does to a floating word.

pairs.left: Name the facts and the earlier knowledge
pairs.right: Restores the concept to its context
Adds emphasis, and leaves the word floating

pairs.left: Add a thicker abstraction and no facts
pairs.right: Floats it further from the base

pairs.left: Stipulate a new meaning and drop the units
pairs.right: Replaces the concept instead of restoring it

feedback.note: The repair goes downward, to facts and to earlier knowledge. Emphasis stays on the surface. A thicker word with no facts is another floating concept piled on the first. A stipulation that drops the units does not put the original concept back, because the referents that gave it meaning have been discarded. Restoration keeps those units and reconnects them.

feedback.note: Restoration names the facts and the earlier knowledge. Volume, sincerity, and a slogan do not restore a concept, because none of them is the context the word was cut off from. Emphasis leaves it floating. Only the connection to referents and to the order of knowledge puts the meaning back.

exercises.prompt: A definition is restated to a deeper characteristic, and the same units are kept. Is that the repair of a floating concept, or a different act?

choices.text: The same act. Any new sentence about a word counts as putting it back, even when the units have been dropped
The same act, because dropping the units is what restatement means, the referents cut away on purpose
A different act. It deepens a concept that still has its units. Restoration is for a word cut off from its units
Neither, because concepts cannot be reconnected to facts once spoken, later naming powerless to restore it

feedback.note: A contextual restatement keeps the units and changes which characteristic is cited as fundamental. Restoring a floating concept reconnects a detached word to facts and to earlier knowledge. They are different acts. Dropping the units would be neither, because both the restatement and the restoration are supposed to hold onto the referents rather than discard them.

exercises.prompt: Which attempt looks like a repair and still leaves the concept floating?

choices.text: Pointing to the tables a person meant by furniture, beds included
Citing the measurements a certainty was based on, percepts included
Naming the earlier concept a wider word integrates, percepts too
Saying "I really mean it" and still refusing to name a fact

feedback.note: Pointing, citing evidence, and naming the earlier concept all reconnect the word to its context. "I really mean it" adds sincerity and no fact. The concept stays floating, because emphasis is not a body of knowledge. The attempt looks like commitment and leaves the detachment untouched. Meaning is not restored by insisting. It is restored by the facts.

exercises.prompt: Build the repair that goes down to the base rather than up into emphasis.

feedback.note: To put a concept back, name the facts and the earlier knowledge. Volume and a thicker slogan do not do it, because they add no context. They leave the word floating or float it further. The repair is a return to the referents and to the order, not an increase in emphasis and not a new stipulation that drops the units.

exercises.prompt: What two questions check a concept for context and for order at once?

choices.text: What knowledge does it depend on, and is that knowledge earlier rather than denied
How loudly it was said, and whether the room agreed, volume and assent being the test
Does it feel certain, and does a story make it welcome, comfort replacing dependence
Can it cancel percepts, and can it float with no facts, cancellation treated as success

feedback.note: The check asks what knowledge the concept depends on, and whether that knowledge is earlier in the order and is being used as earlier. Volume and a nod are not the check, because they supply no context. A feeling or a welcome story is subjectivism. Cancelling percepts, or floating with no facts, is what the check is designed to catch, not what it recommends.

exercises.prompt: "The sample is acidic" is based on an indicator and on earlier knowledge of what that indicator means. Do the two questions pass?

choices.text: No. Any use of earlier knowledge is an inversion, hierarchy made impossible by that order
Yes. The dependence is named, and the earlier knowledge is used rather than denied
No. An indicator is a percept, so it cannot support a later claim, color barred
Yes, but only if a vote adopts the color, the color admitted only by vote

feedback.note: The claim depends on the indicator result and on earlier knowledge of what the indicator means. That knowledge is earlier, and the claim uses it. Both questions pass. Treating every use of a base as an inversion would make hierarchy impossible, because later knowledge is supposed to rest on earlier knowledge. The failure is denial of the base, or a failure to name it, not the dependence itself.

exercises.prompt: "Language proves we have no sensory evidence." Apply both questions. Where does the claim fail?

choices.text: It fails because language was spoken softly, softness being what the check actually catches
It passes, because a later item may cancel whatever it rests on, later items cancelling their base
Language depends on concepts and on sensory evidence, and the claim denies that earlier base
It fails only because no vote was taken, a missing vote being the only defect

feedback.note: The first question has an answer: language depends on concepts, which depend on sensory evidence. The second question fails, because that earlier knowledge is being denied rather than used. The claim inverts the order. Softness and a missing vote are irrelevant, because the fault is hierarchical. A later item cannot be the proof that its own base does not exist.

exercises.prompt: Match each claim to the result of the two questions.

pairs.left: Acid, from a named indicator and its known meaning
pairs.right: Passes: dependence named, and the earlier knowledge is used

pairs.left: Language used to deny sensory evidence
pairs.right: Fails the order: the earlier base is denied

pairs.left: "Be objective," meaning take no side and naming no facts
pairs.right: Fails the first question: no knowledge is named as the dependence

pairs.left: A formula traced back to the measurements it used
pairs.right: Passes: the later item is kept in its place in the order

feedback.note: The check has two parts, and a claim can fail either. Acid and the traced formula name earlier knowledge and use it as earlier, so they pass. Language denying sensory evidence names a base and then cancels it, which inverts the order. "Be objective" with no facts fails the first question, because a floating word has no stated dependence to inspect.

exercises.prompt: Complete the two questions of the check, in order.

parts.text: What does it depend on, and is that knowledge

feedback.note: The second question asks whether the knowledge depended on is earlier in the order, and whether it is being used as earlier rather than denied. Louder, kinder, and newer are not positions in that order. A newer item is the dependent one, not the base. The check fails a claim that treats the newer item as if it came first, because later knowledge rests on earlier knowledge.

exercises.prompt: A politician says "justice" and, when asked what it depends on, answers "on justice itself," naming no act and no fact. Which question fails, and how?

choices.text: Neither. A word that depends only on itself is the base of the order, self-reference as the base
The second only. The facts are earlier, and he is using them, despite no fact having been named
Both pass, because repetition of the word is a context, repetition counted as the body of facts
The first. He has not named any knowledge the word depends on, so the concept is floating

feedback.note: A concept that "depends on itself," with no facts and no earlier ideas, has not been given a context. The first question fails, and the word is floating. It is not a base of the order. Repetition is not a context, because context is the body of facts and earlier knowledge a claim depends on. Until those are named, the second question has nothing to inspect.

exercises.prompt: Science is cited, the experiments are named, and then the conclusion says those experiments cannot be known. Which question fails?

choices.text: The second. The dependence is named and then denied, so the later conclusion attacks its base
The first. No dependence was named, the citation somehow still naming nothing
Neither. Naming experiments and denying them is ordinary adherence, denial called adherence
The first, because experiments are not knowledge, a measurement barred from counting as knowledge

feedback.note: Unlike a floating slogan, this conclusion names what it depends on, so the first question is answered. The second fails: the experiments are earlier, and the conclusion denies them. That is an inversion of the order, the same fault as using a concept while rejecting the base that gives it meaning. Adherence would have used the experiments as evidence, not as a ladder to kick away.

exercises.prompt: Build the check so that both questions stay in force.

feedback.note: The check asks what knowledge the concept depends on, and whether that knowledge is earlier in the order. Louder is emphasis, which restores nothing. Optional would allow a later item to float free of its base or to cancel it. Both moves fail the check, because context and hierarchy are one demand: name the earlier knowledge, and do not use the concept against it.
